public_rationale: The Brussels Privacy Hub’s 6 December 2021 analysis identifies a November 2021 compromise under the Slovenian Council presidency and reports that it expressly excluded general-purpose AI systems from the Act’s scope [e2]. The French presidency’s 16 May 2022 report describes revising existing general-purpose AI provisions [e3]. The earlier Slovenian text contradicts the claimed French first mention under the contract’s definition, which includes express exclusions [e2, e3].
limitations: The evidence does not identify the individual or national delegation that first suggested the wording.
An earlier mention establishes the contradiction without establishing the absolute first mention in the legislative process.
This assessment does not establish who first proposed direct obligations for foundation-model providers or whether anyone knowingly made a false statement.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: The first mention of foundation models in the EU AI Act process came from the French government.

statement.document_title: Meta’s Chief AI Officer is lying about the EU AI Act

from_speaker: The first mention of foundation models
sometimes referred to as General Purpose AI
our_interpretation: Read 'first mention' as the first express treatment of general-purpose AI in an AI Act proposal or negotiating text, including provisions specifying exclusions.
Read 'French government' as France acting through the French Council presidency.
The historical comparison covers the proposal and negotiations through May 2022, the claimed time of introduction. It starts with the Commission proposal on 21 April 2021.
The claim concerns who introduced the subject, rather than who first proposed direct obligations for general-purpose AI providers.
criteria.support_condition: The earliest relevant negotiating text expressly addressing general-purpose AI originated with the French Council presidency, with no earlier qualifying text from another presidency or institution.
criteria.contradiction_condition: An earlier negotiating text from another presidency or institution expressly addressed general-purpose AI before the French presidency's May 2022 intervention.

evidence.excerpt:
The changes in the document compared with the Commission's proposal are underlined:
additions are marked with bold, deletions with strikethrough.
evidence.locator: Introduction, paragraph 6; provenance in paragraphs 2–5; substantive additions in section II.6 and Article 52a
evidence.explanation: The document identifies the Slovenian presidency's compromise and explains how additions are marked. Section II.6 expressly identifies new general-purpose AI provisions, including Article 52a, demonstrating treatment of the subject before the French intervention.

evidence.excerpt: In addition, the Council version excludes all “general purpose AI systems” from the scope of the AIA.
evidence.locator: Opening discussion, paragraph beginning 'First of all'
evidence.explanation: The report identifies the reviewed compromise as the Slovenian presidency's November text and explicitly discusses its general-purpose AI provision. This contemporary corroboration confirms that the subject was already present and publicly discussed in 2021.

evidence.excerpt:
These amendments aim to ensure a fair distribution of responsibilities and a level
playing field throughout the AI value chain.
evidence.explanation: This section describes the French presidency revising general-purpose AI provisions to rebalance providers' obligations. It supports France's substantive involvement in May 2022, while describing amendments rather than the subject's first appearance.
